title: Expressing & Justifying Opinions
keyIdea: An opinion is what you think or feel about something. To justify it, give a reason that tells why: I think … because …. A good reason is about the opinion (not off topic), says something new (not just I just do or it is good), and is clear enough for the listener to picture. Others may think differently; we can agree or disagree kindly and give our own reason.

kid: An opinion is what you think. I think dogs are fun. Your friend may think cats are more fun. Both are fine.
Say why with the word because. I think dogs are fun because they play with me. The part after because is the reason.
Because I just do is not a reason. It does not tell why. Because it is good does not tell much. Say the thing you like: it has a funny dragon in it.
When a friend says what they think, you can agree or not. Be kind. Say I agree because, or I disagree because, and give your reason.
adult: This is spoken language in England's National Curriculum. Pupils should articulate and justify answers, arguments and opinions. They also take part in discussions, role play and debates. Development Matters asks children of three and four to express a point of view and to debate when they disagree. In Reception they connect one idea to another using connectives such as because. US Common Core asks kindergarten children to state an opinion or preference (W.K.1). Grade 1 adds a reason and some sense of closure (W.1.1).

The sentence stem I think … because … gives children the structure. The opinion comes first. The conjunction because brings in the reason. A longer turn can add a second reason with and, then close with So …. The stems I agree because and I disagree because teach children to answer the idea, not the person.

Common mistakes: an opinion with no reason, a circular reason (I like it because I like it, or because I just do), a reason that is true but off topic, a vague reason (it is good, it is nice), and disagreeing by attacking the speaker (you are wrong!) instead of giving a different reason. Children also often think that if two people disagree, one of them must be wrong; with opinions, both can have good reasons.

In the lab your child drags word cards into a speech bubble to build I think … because …, picks reasons that really explain, swaps vague reasons for clear ones, answers a friend kindly, and builds a short talk with two reasons and an ending.

familyTip: At dinner, ask a which-do-you-like-best question (which pudding, which park, which book). When your child answers, smile and ask: why do you think that? Then share your own opinion with a because.

visual.caption: I think the park is fun because… Is it a real reason? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: I can go on the swings
I can run on the grass

lab.caption: Flagship lab: build I think … because … in a speech bubble, pick real and clear reasons, answer a friend kindly, and give a short opinion talk.

practice.prompt: Which one gives an opinion and a reason?
choices: I think snow is fun because I can make a snowman.
Snow is fun because it is fun.
practice.hint: Look for the word because, and a reason that tells why.
practice.explain: It says what you think (snow is fun) and why (I can make a snowman). The others have no reason, or say the same thing again.

practice.prompt: {n} children each say one opinion with one reason. How many times do you hear the word because?
practice.hint: Each child uses because once, to bring in the reason.
practice.explain: Each of the {n} children says because once, so you hear it {n} times.

practice.prompt: I like my teddy because… Which reason is the clearest?
choices: he is soft and I cuddle him at night.
practice.hint: Which one helps you picture why the teddy is special?
practice.explain: Soft and cuddled at night tells us why. He is good says very little, and I just do is not a reason.

practice.prompt: {n} children give an opinion. {k} of them forget to say why. How many gave a reason?
practice.hint: Take away the children who gave no reason.
practice.explain: {n} take away {k} is {=n-k}, so {=n-k} children gave a reason.

pool.prompt: Which word do we use to give a reason?
pool.hint: I think it is fun … it has a slide.
pool.explain: Because joins the opinion to the reason: I think it is fun because it has a slide.

pool.prompt: Sam says: I think frogs are cool because I just do. What is missing?
pool.hint: He says what he thinks. Does he say why?
pool.explain: I just do does not tell why, so a real reason is missing, like because they can jump so far.

pool.prompt: I think summer is the best because… Which reason fits?
choices: I can swim in the sea.
pool.hint: The reason must be about summer and tell why.
pool.explain: Swimming in the sea is about summer and tells why. A shoe is off topic, and it is says nothing.

pool.prompt: Zoe says: I think carrots are yummy because they are crunchy. What is a kind way to disagree?
choices: I disagree, because I like soft food more.
Carrots are yucky, you are wrong!
pool.hint: Be kind and give your own reason.
pool.explain: I disagree, because… is kind and gives a reason. You are wrong is not kind, and No gives no reason.

pool.prompt: Ben likes rain and Ella does not. Who is wrong?
choices: Nobody: they can both have reasons
pool.hint: Is this a fact or what each one thinks?
pool.explain: These are opinions. Ben and Ella can think different things and both give good reasons.

pool.prompt: Ali gives {a} reasons for liking the zoo and {b} more reasons for liking the farm. How many reasons is that?
pool.hint: Put the zoo reasons and the farm reasons together.

pool.prompt: In a group of {n}, everyone gives an opinion and {k} children also say I agree with a reason. How many did not say I agree?
pool.hint: Take the children who agreed away from the group.
pool.explain: {n} take away {k} is {=n-k}, so {=n-k} children did not say I agree.

pool.prompt: Which ending fits a short opinion talk about pandas?
pool.hint: An ending says the opinion again with So.
pool.explain: So pandas are my favourite! closes the talk by saying the opinion again.
